power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.149", "p = 0.085"), Sentence = c("While no such effect was found in Experiment 1 (Figure 4A, exp(β) = -0.02, t = -1.44, p = 0.149), we observed shorter saccade latencies under high load in Experiment 2 (Figure 4B, exp(β) = -0.05, t = -4.12, p < 0.001), consistent with participants shortening deeper elaboration under load (Wilkinson notation: latency ∼ load + (1 + load | participant) + (1 | direction)).", "Yet, we found no interaction between this and experiment (exp(β) = -0.03, t = -1.72, p = 0.085; Wilkinson notation: latency ∼ experi-ment * load + (1 + load | participant) + (1 | direction))." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Departing from traditional information-maximization accounts, recent work proposes that saccade selection arbitrates economically between the expected benefits and costs of shifting attention.
We tested this economic account by manipulating the cognitive resources available during selection, arguing that reduced resources should increase the weight of costs, thereby altering selection.
Across two experiments, participants selected between saccade targets while performing a non-spatial memory task that manipulated cognitive load.
Targets appeared in directions with previously and independently established intrinsic (effort) costs, quantified through pupillometry.
In Experiment 1, monetary rewards were staircased against participants' choices, replicating that money can compensate for intrinsic costs.
This yielded an informative reward range from which Experiment 2 sampled randomly.
Experiment 2 revealed that higher memory load biased selection toward cost-efficient saccades, while reward sensitivity remained unaffected.
Load also selectively shortened the long latency tail, consistent with reduced deliberation under increased load and therefore an increased weight on deliberation cost.
Saccade selection thus depends on available cognitive resources, supporting an economic account of visual selection over information maximization accounts.
Humans redirect their eyes several times per second, rapidly moving the eyes (socalled saccades) to bring task-relevant information onto the fovea, where it can be processed in detail.
Saccade selection is traditionally understood as reflecting the physical salience of visual stimuli, the history of previous selections, and the observer's current goals [1].

Together, this evidence motivates the hypothesis that saccade selection depends on available cognitive resources.

The central fixation dot was a black ring (1° diameter) presented on a screen-centered circle (12° radius, gray ≈42.4 cd/m 2 ).

Participants then selected a target by making an eye movement toward it.

Recent work has proposed that saccade selection follows an economic principle, weighing the costs of shifting gaze against the rewards available at alternative locations.
We reasoned that if saccade selection draws on a limited cognitive budget, concurrent memory load should alter how costs and rewards are weighed.
We found evidence for two out of three predictions.
First, non-spatial load made saccade choices more cost driven, consistent with these costs being computed relative to the available resources.
Second, load selectively curtailed the prolonged decisions that reflect deeper deliberation, shortening the upper tail of the latency distribution.
In contrast, we found no evidence for non-specific interference of load with optimal selection.
Together, this suggests that load does not degrade selection in-discriminately, but recalibrates how strongly saccade costs are weighed and how much deliberation each choice is worth.

text.text: Such effects are compatible with several accounts, because they do not separate costs from other determinants of selection.

We here demonstrate that load selectively reshaped selection: the weight of previously established, physiologically-inferred intrinsic saccade costs increased under load, while reward sensitivity was unaffected.
This pattern is predicted by the economic model and indicates that load does not degrade selection, but changes the relative weighting of its determinants.
In other words, selection remains optimal, but input variables change.
Likely, many global load effects on gaze can thus be understood parsimoniously as reweighting of costs within visual selection.
The economic model further holds that decision-making is itself costly.
Elaborating longer means higher costs [32], and should thus only be recruited when its expected utility gains exceed that cost [6].
text.formatted: Elaborating longer means higher costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>, and should thus only be recruited when its expected utility gains exceed that cost <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: This idea has a long history in economics, where decision costs are thought to limit how much information is processed [33, 34], and work which describes how simple heuristics can match or outperform exhaustive deliberation [35, 36].
text.formatted: This idea has a long history in economics, where decision costs are thought to limit how much information is processed <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34]</ref>, and work which describes how simple heuristics can match or outperform exhaustive deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36]</ref>.

text.text: The empirical basis for this account to apply to visual selection as suggested in Strauch et al. [6] has been limited thus far, however.
text.formatted: The empirical basis for this account to apply to visual selection as suggested in Strauch et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> has been limited thus far, however.

text.text: Our latency data speak to this in two ways: Wider utility gaps should come with more elaborate (and thus longer) decisions.
Indeed, the larger utility gaps in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1, where they were minimized by design, were associated with longer latencies.
Second, load selectively shortened the prolonged decisions of Ex-periment 2 while leaving short decisions unaffected.
This is to be expected when the value of deliberation drops under reduced resources due to an increased weight of deliberation costs.
Both findings thus support the assumption that decision depth during saccade selection is itself decided economically.
In principle, shorter latencies under load could also reflect memory-induced urgency to reach recall sooner.
Such hurrying, however, should make choices noisier, weakening the mapping of both costs and rewards onto selection.
Instead, reward mapping was unaffected and cost mapping became steeper rather than flatter under load.
Both findings are thus incompatible with an urgency account, but in line with economic adjustment of decision depth.
Additionally, were memory-induced urgency truly present, we assume its effect would have been present in both experiments.
Still, latencies are not uniquely determined by decision depth.
The findings are therefore consistent with reduced deliberation under higher load, but do not conclusively establish that interpretation.
Task load induced in the present experiments was arguably relatively low, as expressed in the overall good performance in the color reports.
Future work could thus extend the present data by inducing stronger load, which should increase effect sizes on visual selection in the same directions as observed here.
Load should affect visual selection as a whole [6] and not just saccades (which are easiest to study).
text.formatted: Load should affect visual selection as a whole <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> and not just saccades (which are easiest to study).

text.text: Indeed, load likewise affects eye movements ranging from smooth pursuit deviations [22] to microsaccade rates and beyond [23, 37].
text.formatted: Indeed, load likewise affects eye movements ranging from smooth pursuit deviations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> to microsaccade rates and beyond <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37]</ref>.

text.text: Costs further constrain fixation selection in natural tasks [38], suggesting that the load-induced cost reweighting observed here generalizes to everyday viewing.
text.formatted: Costs further constrain fixation selection in natural tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>, suggesting that the load-induced cost reweighting observed here generalizes to everyday viewing.

text.text: Consequently, establishing cost differences among such attention shift types should allow for specific predictions about the alterations that occur under increased load.
Lastly, effects such as induced here through additional load, should equally occur when resources become more limited for different reasons.
For instance, beginning cognitive decline may keep visual selection optimal, but change the weight of costs on the side of input variables.
Similar effects may be producible due to exhaustion or tiredness, all effects that remain to be tested as of today.
Understanding eye movement behavior can thus, in turn, provide insights into the amount of available resources and reward of the observer as an instantiation of high throughput decision-making.
Ideally, such understanding would allow for models that incorporate the observers' individual resource budget and cost representations.

Intrinsic cost estimates already improve computational gaze prediction [14], and the present findings show that the resource budget and weighing could help individualize such models beyond one-size-fits-all approaches [see also 39].
text.formatted: Intrinsic cost estimates already improve computational gaze prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, and the present findings show that the resource budget and weighing could help individualize such models beyond one-size-fits-all approaches [see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39]</ref>.

text.text: Together, we tested a central difference between information maximization and economic accounts of selection that factor in costs: only an economic account predicts changes with available resources.
Under load, saccade costs gained weight while reward sensitivity was unaffected.
Furthermore, prolonged decisions were particularly cut short under load, suggesting that arbitration depth is itself decided economically.
Selection thus does not merely maximize information gain, but does so relative to costs in a variable budget.
This opens the door to better predictions of selection across situations and individuals.

Existing load studies demonstrate effects on gaze allocation, but they have not tested whether load selectively reshapes preferences between saccades with physiologically established saccade costs.
Using such cost-characterized saccade directions allows us to ask not only whether load changes saccade selection, but also how it changes the relation between saccade costs, rewards, and selection.
More importantly, an economic account of visual selection, combined with recently established intrinsic saccade costs [6, 15, 16] predicts how selection should change as a function of higher load.
Using the same target configuration as in Koevoet et al. [16], we therefore tested whether and how concurrent memory load alters selection, drawing on already established physiological saccade costs.
If saccade selection is truly resource-bound, concurrent memory load should alter saccade preferences.

We distinguish three possible routes through which load could affect selection: Cost reweighting (economic prediction): Load may increase the relative weight of saccade costs, leading to stronger preferences for lower-cost targets.
Non-specific interference (alternative): Load may impair selection non-specifically, increasing choice variability and weakening the relation between selection, cost, and reward.
Reduced deliberation (economic prediction):Load may reduce investment in deliberative arbitration, yielding coarser selection and fewer prolonged decisions.
Figure1: Possible effects of load on saccade selection.
A Economic prediction: Load could increase the relative weight of costs, thus shifting selection towards cost minimization at the expense of reward maximization.
We found evidence for this effect.
B Alternative: Load could reduce resources for deliberation during selection nonspecifically and thus may make selection noisier, weakening the link between costs and rewards with selection.
We found no evidence for such general interference under load.
C Economic prediction: Load could reduce investment in deliberative cost-benefit weighing, selectively reducing prolonged choices in the upper tail of the latency distribution.
We found stronger shortening of long latencies under load.
Figure2: Experimental paradigm and core findings from Experiment 1.
A Participants were blockwise tasked to either memorize ("high-load trials") two subsequently presented colors or to not memorize ("low-load trials") the presented colors (each followed by a mask).
After this, participants performed a free-choice task to assess saccade preferences.
A new trial was initiated by fixating on a central fixation dot, upon which two possible saccade targets were presented on the screen for selection.
Following ten successful trials, participants were asked for response on the color recall task (either by clicking on the color ring or on the inside of the color ring).
B Rewards were updated dynamically.
C Saccade costs were linked to the final obtained reward structure.
D Empirically observed reward differences in Experiment 1, providing a suitable reward range for Experiment 2.
